content.thinking:
I need to write this whole file in one pass without tool verification, so I'm being careful to get the API right from memory. I'm designing a treasure hoard prop group with a League of Legends-style aesthetic — exaggerated dynamic shapes, saturated high-contrast accents, and glowing magic effects readable from a top-down camera — while making sure the structure still satisfies the builder's requirement of exactly one root joint.

I'm planning a root joint at the origin plus a hinge joint for the chest lid, then sketching rough dimensions: a chest around 0.7m wide and 0.45m tall, a coin mound spanning 1.6m, a crown and goblets scaled down, aiming for an overall height near 0.8m with everything resting on y=0. Now I'm laying out the base dais as a lathe-generated stone disc with a glowing rune ring for top-down readability.

The rune ring will be a flat textured plane with magenta and cyan strokes sitting just above the base surface, and the base itself uses a lathe profile with cobblestone-style patch texturing in dark purple. I'm weighing stylization choices like cel shading versus paint for a League-of-Legends-inspired look, keeping in mind that painted parts can't glow so I need to reserve paint for non-emissive surfaces.

For the gold elements, I'm planning to use cel shading with a bright gold highlight and a hue-shifted shadow tone, plus scales-based texturing to mimic coin disc patterns on a lathe-built coin mound, bumping paint resolution to 2048 to keep detail sharp given the larger painted surface area.

Then for individual coins, I'm scattering many small cylinders across the mound with random tilts and positions, merging them by color group (three gold tones plus silver) using mergeGeometries after applying transform matrices to each instance -- this keeps draw calls low while still looking like a scattered pile, with some coins standing on edge or stacked near the base for variety.

Now I'm figuring out the overall composition: placing the dais at the origin with the chest sitting toward the back, and working out the chest's dimensions and how the lid opens backward on a hinge so it reads as flung open with treasure spilling forward toward the viewer.

Working out the formula, θ=−105° swings the lid up past vertical, landing at y'≈0.97 and z'≈−0.26 — tipped back over the hinge as intended.

I should build everything in closed position first, then apply the pose rotation at the very end, since the lid's child parts and sweeps are modeled in local coordinates before the hinge transform. The interior pieces stay attached to the root bone so they're unaffected. Estimating the open-lid height: with hinge at y≈0.31 and lid depth plus dome around 0.37, the top of the open lid reaches roughly 0.68.

For the hinge joint itself, I need the lid joint parented to root at that hinge position, with a direction vector so the bone runs correctly along the lid's length—orienting it to point forward so parts without explicit bone assignment snap to the nearest joint appropriately.

Since a childless joint like the lid might only register as a point, I'm considering making every part explicit about which bone it belongs to, using a helper that pairs position and bone assignment together to avoid accidental misattachment.

I need to pick the right imports—Fill and PartOptions from context/parts, V3 from math—while avoiding unused import errors. For the actual geometry, I'm planning to use lathe for turned shapes like goblets and vases, extrude for crown spikes and decorations, and sweep for handles, straps, and rims.

For gems, I'm considering using flat-shaded Octahedron, Icosahedron, and Dodecahedron geometries with distinct colors like ruby, sapphire, emerald, and amethyst, and thinking through how glow interacts with flat shading—since emissive at full strength plus lit facets might wash out the faceted look, so I may need a different approach to preserve the gem's faceted appearance while still glowing.

I'll only merge matching geometry types together — polyhedra with polyhedra, since they share the same non-indexed structure — keeping big gems as separate parts and merging small scatter gems by color. Mixed octahedron/dodecahedron merges should still work since all polyhedron geometries are non-indexed, and the resulting merged mesh can still take the glow treatment as a single Part.

For the coin pile, rather than a lathe shape, I'll build the mound as several overlapping squashed-sphere lumps colored gold, with the coins scattered on top to hide the underlying shape. To place coins realistically I need a height function defining the mound surface — treating each lump as an ellipsoid cap and taking the max height across all lumps at a given x,z position.

Switching to half-ellipsoid domes built from lathe geometry so they sit flush with the floor instead of sinking below it, defining the lathe outline from the axis up to the rim.

Adding smaller side lumps, then thinking about how to fill the chest with an overflowing pile of coins — placing a rounded heap lump near the chest's rim so it reads as spilling coins rather than a flat interior.

I'll approximate surface normals numerically using the height gradient for coin orientation. For scattering coins, I'm placing random points across the ground region, rejecting ones below a height threshold or inside the chest's footprint, letting the heap's main lump overlap the chest front slightly so it partially conceals it.

Now I need to handle coins that pile inside the chest itself, treating the fill region as its own ellipsoid with separate center, radius, and base height parameters so I can unify it with the ground lumps in one general height function.

Actually to make it an open chest I should build it from four thin wall boxes plus a bottom, leaving the interior visible with the coin dome filling it near rim level, using wall thickness 0.03 and interior dimensions roughly ±0.28 by ±0.15.

For the wood texture, I'll use a grain paint wrapped in a cel shader for toon-style shading, picking a bold mystical palette — warm gold lit tones with darker shadow and edge colors, paired with deep brown wood tones for the chest body.

Now I'm working out the rest of the palette: dark steel-violet straps with gold studs for contrast, a purple stone dais with teal and magenta rune glow, and a set of vivid gem colors (ruby, sapphire, emerald, amethyst, topaz, diamond) to scatter across the design.

I'm also planning extra hoard details like a crown with velvet cushion, jeweled goblets with glowing magical liquid, a coin sack, and a pearl necklace to round out the treasure pile.

Now I'm sketching the overall layout on the dais, placing the chest at the back center, a main coin heap in front of it, and smaller heaps and props arranged around them with specific positions and sizes.

I'm adding a right-side heap, a stacked gold bar prop with layered height, and a tied coin sack placed off to the left with its own color scheme and rope detail.

Then for the crown, I'm placing it upright near the heap's apex, sinking it slightly into the coins and tilting it forward a bit so it looks naturally rested rather than floating.

Designing the crown geometry in detail: a gold base ring, seven alternating tall and short spikes with pointed curved outlines rising to gem-tipped peaks, each extruded along the ring's tangent and radial directions so they sweep outward realistically.

I'm adding small gem accents around the band at regular angles, plus torus rings for the top and bottom rims rotated to lie flat against the crown's circular form. I'm planning a larger jeweled centerpiece gem on the front with a glow effect, reminiscent of ornate crown designs.

I'm sketching two crossing arcs made from smooth curved sweeps that rise from the band to meet at the top, topped with a glowing orb, plus a velvet-red domed interior visible through the gaps between the arches.

Still defining goblet profile...

I'm checking that the inner wall never crosses the outer profile at each y-level, confirming the stem and axis closures stay valid, and considering whether to leave smoothing at its default of 0 for sharp corners.

For the goblets I'm sketching a glowing liquid disc inside goblet 2 using a thin cylinder sized to match the inner wall radius near the rim, with a magenta or cyan glow for a potion effect. I'm also planning the four-goblet arrangement: a gold one standing on the heap, a silver one standing, and one tipped over spilling coins using a rotated lathe shape.

Working out the orientation for the tipped goblet, placing its foot on the heap with the axis angled so it lies on its side, resting at the right height above the surface, with coins scattered in a line from the mouth to suggest they spilled out.

I'm also planning the gem-studded goblet: a gold cup ringed by six small gems plus decorative torus bands at the stem knob and rim. For all standing goblets, I need to compute their resting height from the heap surface, sinking the foot slightly into the pile for realism.

Now I'm placing specific pieces: a gold goblet on the side lump, a silver one with a purple-gemmed cup holding a potion on the right lump, and a larger ruby-studded gold goblet resting on the dais floor, each positioned with the right sink depth for its surface.

Then I'm working out the tipped goblet spilling coins onto the dais, oriented mouth-first with coins cascading outward, and double-checking that all the heap lumps and the main coin pile stay within the dais's radius so nothing overhangs the edge.

I'm scattering roughly 28 small gems of varying sizes across the heaps, then placing three glowing crystal spire clusters in teal, violet, and pink behind the chest on the dais to add vertical accents to the treasure pile.

I realize the open chest lid would block the crystal clusters if placed directly behind it, so I'm repositioning them to the left and right flanks instead, away from the lid's swing path and clear of the bars, while shifting the coin sack to sit beside them for balance.

I'm adjusting the side lumps' positions slightly to avoid overlapping the gold bars too much, shifting them to z=0.2-0.22 with reduced radii. Now I'm checking the main heap lump's placement relative to the dais edge, finding it's a bit too tight and considering increasing the dais radius to around 1.05 to give more clearance.

Working through sizing now—the dais at 2.1m diameter feels large relative to the smaller props (crown, goblets, chest), so I'm scaling back to radius 0.95 and repositioning the heap lumps accordingly: main lump pulled closer to center, two side lumps smaller, and a couple small front lumps for spill texture, though I'm reconsidering whether those smaller lumps are even needed given the tipped goblet placement nearby.

I'm scattering loose coins near the dais edges instead—three coin stacks at different counts and positions, plus one coin standing on its edge for visual interest. I'm also double-checking the vertical stacking: dais top at 0.05m baseline, heap and chest sitting on that surface, open lid rising to about 0.68m with the hinge geometry, and crystals topping out near 0.5m, giving an overall scene height around 0.7m.

Now I'm working out the chest's box geometry: centering it at z=-0.2 with outer half-width 0.32 and half-depth 0.19, wall thickness 0.03. I'm defining the four wall panels (front, back, two sides) and the bottom panel with their box dimensions and positions, then placing an interior fill ellipsoid to represent the chest's hollow space.

I'm considering using only the top hemisphere of the sphere geometry for the fill, since the bottom half would be hidden inside the box anyway and painting it would waste texture space.

For the coin pile shape, I'm defining an elliptical lump centered at the back of the chest, computing a squared distance from this center scaled by its radii to determine the height at each point.

Now I'm restricting coin placement so they don't spawn through the chest walls, sampling positions separately within each lump's ellipse to keep coins confined to valid fill regions.

Checking if that lump overlaps the chest's rim slightly, I figure the coin height there still clips under the wall acceptably. I should just reject any coin that falls inside the chest's outer bounding box unless it belongs to a chest-adjacent lump, so coins don't appear embedded in the model.

Working out coin counts across heaps: 150 main, 60 and 50 for the two smaller piles, 70 filling the chest, totaling 330 coins, each a low-poly cylinder around 40 triangles, keeping the total well under budget alongside gems and other props. I'll merge coins by color into a handful of mesh groups, and orient each one by tilting its cylinder axis off the surface normal with a random rotation so some coins lie flat while others stick up on edge for a natural scattered look.

Mapping coin texture onto cylinder sides...

I'll make three color variants per coin texture, each with a darker outer rim ring, inner ring line, and star, tinting via a color parameter rather than flat painting. For gems, instead of texturing I'm considering faceted geometry like a scaled octahedron or dodecahedron, or possibly a lathe-generated crown-and-pavilion gem cut shape for a more classic look.

Still writing lathe profile...

Each lathe builds its own mesh so parts can't easily merge, which affects my part budget—maybe 400 total between big faceted gems and scattered small ones. Glow needs a single flat material, so I'll use lathes for the bigger gems and consider merged polyhedra for the small scattered ones to keep part counts cheap.

Estimating total parts: coin merges to 3, gems add ~28 individual lathe shapes with shared cached glow materials, each lathe is cheap geometry at roughly 60 triangles. For orientation, I'll write a gem function that scales an outline by size, tilts along a random axis, and sinks it slightly into its placement point so it reads as embedded rather than floating; I also need to set up the rng and tune glow strength so it doesn't wash out the faceting.

Now I'm working out the chest lid geometry relative to the hinge point, treating it as a barrel vault—essentially a half-cylinder opened to the correct arc length and radius to match the box's depth, rotated onto the right axis, built either from a partial cylinder geometry or a custom extruded arch outline.

Tracing points for the half-ellipse arc from π to 0, closing the base with a flat line, forming a solid half-ellipse prism with a small bevel.

Now I need to paint the underside face a deep crimson for the interior lining, distinguishing it from the wall faces by checking which points sit near the base (s[1] close to zero) versus the side caps.

But baking cel shading at build time creates a problem for the lid: since lighting/normals are computed in the build pose, if I build it closed then rotate it open, the shading will look wrong because the "lit" surfaces no longer face the actual light direction. The fix is to build the lid directly in its open orientation so the baked shading matches the final pose, similar to how the tipped goblet needs to be built with its final axis orientation from the start.

I need a rotation helper that maps closed-local coordinates to world positions through the hinge, handling boxes with quaternions, extrudes by rotating their direction vectors, and sweeps by rotating their point arrays, all around a defined hinge point and rotation angle.

Actually, I realize I can simplify by building parts directly in the open pose and placing the lid joint at the hinge pointing along the open direction, so the rig itself starts open and a rigger can rotate it closed later — no separate pose transform needed.

Now I'm working out the straps across the arch: steel bands swept along the arch's curve using a box cross-section, figuring out the binormal direction so the band width runs sideways along x while following the arch profile in the yz plane.

Working out the arch band positions along the lid curve, then planning two side bands plus end rim plates, a metal rim along the front edge, and hinge barrel cylinders at the back corners.

For the lid's wood, I'll apply the grain texture with streaks running along the x-axis to simulate planks spanning the width, keeping the painting simple in world coordinates since the lid is posed open. For ornamentation, I'm placing a gold shield-shaped lock plate with a central gem at the front edge of the lid, where the hasp would meet the body's lock mechanism when closed.

For the chest body, I'm adding gold corner caps as vertical boxes, steel horizontal straps across the front and sides, and small gold rivet spheres merged by color group along those straps. The lock itself gets a gold plate on the front with a dark keyhole decal (ellipse plus slot) and a gem set into it.

Now I'm working out the lid hasp geometry — a tongue shape that hangs down over the front lock plate when the lid is closed, defining it in the lid's local coordinate frame so it swings correctly with the hinge when the lid opens.

I'm computing where the lid's apex point ends up once rotated open about the hinge axis, working through the rotation matrix for a -105° tilt to find the new y' and z' coordinates, landing the apex near (0, 0.45, -0.635).

Now I'm checking which lid surface faces the viewer once open: the outer arch faces back and stays hidden, while the inner flat underside faces forward-up, so that's the surface I should decorate with crimson velvet and diamond-quilt tufting, likely via an SVG texture mapped onto a plane decal positioned at the lid's interior.

Working through the rotation math confirms the direction vector faces forward correctly, with default world-up orientation being fine. Now I'm considering adding a gold trim frame around the lid's interior perimeter — maybe rods forming a rim at the base of the lid.

Setting up the imports I'll need: Three.js core, geometry merging utilities, the builder and math helpers, path/curve functions, texture and shading kits (grain, paint, toon shading, glow), and type definitions for parts and fills — keeping only what's actually necessary for the scene.

Now I'm scaffolding the build function itself, creating a builder instance for a "Dragon's Treasure Hoard" model with a seeded RNG and a root joint at the origin to anchor the hierarchy.

I'm then adding a hinge joint for the lid, setting up a helper function for placing geometry parts onto the current bone, and defining a gold color palette using the cel function...

Confirming grain defaults to y-axis, so wood on the chest front needs x-axis grain for horizontal planks. Now I'm thinking about adding a painted highlight effect for the gold, crafting a custom paint function that brightens areas facing the key light direction.

Writing the toon shading helper...

Defining more palette tones...

Still writing paint logic...

Finishing the planks function...

Now I'm defining WOOD_A and WOOD_B as celshaded grain textures with slightly different hues and seeds, using the x-axis for grain direction on the chest front walls.

Checking the texture atlas budget — the painted surfaces total around 8 m², giving roughly 1.6mm texel density, which should look sharp enough.

Writing coin SVG textures...

The side texture stretches the whole drawing across its thin band, which gives a noisy but acceptably gold-ish average with some dark streaks reading like a milled edge — good enough. Now defining the color variants: gold A with bright face, amber rim, and darker mark; gold B with a richer face tone; and a silver variant with pale face and rim colors.

Setting up coin geometry and placement...

Checking the lump height formula matches a half-ellipsoid profile correctly, using normalized radial distance squared inside the square root.

I'm reconsidering though—this ellipsoid cap creates a vertical tangent at the rim, which looks unnatural for a heap of coins. A flatter, cone-like falloff near the edge would look more realistic, so I'm testing different exponents on the (1-r²) term to soften the edge slope.

Switching to a parabola profile, y = hy*(1-r²), gives a finite slope at the rim corresponding to roughly a 41° angle, which matches a believable angle of repose for a coin pile. I'll use this parabola for the lathe profile points generating the heap shape, and apply a similar approach for the chest lump separately.

I need the mesh height mismatch resolved — my fill mesh is a hemisphere but the heap profile is parabolic, so coins on top won't align. I'll add a `round` flag to Lump to switch between the ellipsoid sqrt formula and the parabola formula depending on shape. For normals, I'm computing gradients numerically via small finite differences in x and z, then normalizing the resulting vector.

Writing scatter function...

I'm handling overlap between the chest lump and the main heap by excluding coordinates within the chest's bounding box when scattering non-chest lumps, so coins don't double-spawn in that region. For vertical placement, each coin sits slightly above the surface with a small random sink, and its orientation blends the surface normal with random jitter — most coins lie fairly flat, but about 15% get stronger jitter so they appear to stand on edge for visual variety.

Now I'm working out the heap mesh's paint so it blends seamlessly with the coins scattered across it: using a dark-gold scale pattern wrapped in a cel shader so the underlying lathe mound reads as the same metallic gold tone, hiding any gaps between visible coins. I'm positioning the heap mesh vertically relative to the dais top, with a small sink offset so it nestles into the surface correctly.

Still writing the lathe profile...

I'll add a helper to coerce coordinate arrays into the proper tuple type for lathe outlines, then start defining the dais shape using it.

Refining the dais profile into a two-step tapered disc with a chamfered edge, and setting up a stone-like patch pattern for its coloring.

For the top face, I'm planning a glowing rune circle decal positioned flush on the dais surface — a planar texture with concentric rings, twelve glyph ticks, and star-hex lines in cyan and magenta over a transparent background.

I need to nudge the decal height to .056 so it stays visible above the dais but stays hidden beneath the coin heaps where the mound geometry already covers it, letting the textured glow show through naturally around the piled coins.

For the rune's SVG, I'm thinking through resolution tradeoffs — a bigger texture size gives crisper stroke rendering, but that pushes the shared atlas size up, so I need to account for how the paint sheet and texture blocks pack together before deciding on a final size.

Writing SVG rune circles...

I'll bump the minimum stroke width slightly and generate the radial ticks, triangular glyph marks, and hexagram pattern programmatically with cyan, magenta, and gold accents for the glow effect. The chest itself sits on a dais with gilded corner posts.

For the treasure details, I'll add a lock with a large ruby on the chest front, and settle on a final set of elements: crown, four goblets, scattered gems, chest, gold bars, sack, crystals, and a necklace draped across the front of the heap. The necklace path follows the heap's front slope using height-sampled points slightly offset above the surface so it looks like it's resting naturally on the pile.

Still writing geometry...

Setting up helper functions to apply a hinge rotation transform for the lid's local positions and directions, then starting to define the chest's base and top dimensions...

Now I'm defining a wall-building helper that creates boxes with plank-style painted seams, applying horizontal gaps based on vertical position to simulate wooden board joints across the chest's walls, bottom, and feet.

I'm adding gold corner posts with small cube caps at the top and bottom of each post, then placing steel strap bands around the chest body at mid-height to look like reinforcing metal bands.

Still positioning straps...

I'm adding vertical front straps with rivets, plus a central gold lock plate shaped like a shield outline, extruded forward with beveled edges and positioned to sit flush within the wall thickness.

Now I'm defining the shield outline's coordinate points with a sharp bottom point and smoothed side corners, then placing a small dark cylinder keyhole on the plate's front face.

Adding the slot shape and gem placement...

Still defining outline points...

Checking the base face coloring — all its vertices have y=0 so s[1]=0 uniformly across that face, which works fine with the velvet paint logic, and the end caps and arch wall look consistent too. I'm also considering adding a quilted diamond texture plane for the interior, rendering deep crimson diamonds with gold buttons as an SVG decal.

Positioning the quilt plane near the lid's front-facing surface, sized and oriented so its width runs along x and height along the lid's z-direction, with the textured front face pointing outward toward the viewer.

Still working out the gold trim rods around the quilt's perimeter...

Adding more side lips...

For the arch bands, I'll sweep a curved path along the lid's arch using catmull-rom points, generating steel bands on either side with a narrower gold ornamental band down the center.

For rivets, I'm placing merged golden sphere geometry along the band path by sampling points at various t values and offsetting outward, embedding them partially into the band surface with explicit bone binding to the lid. I need to make sure the sweep's frame orientation handles the tilted plane correctly so the box cross-section stays aligned along the right axis.

For the gold end caps on the lid, I'm extruding a slightly enlarged version of the arch outline at each end (x=±0.335), using a thin thickness to form ornamental plates that should slightly overlap the prism's edges for a cleaner seam, while reusing the existing arch outline helper.

Now I'm working out the hinge geometry: small cylinders oriented along the x-axis using a composed quaternion rotation (base orientation times a 90° rotation around Z), placed at the back of the body near the lid's pivot point, with matching steel hinge plates on both the body's back wall and the lid.

For the lid's hasp, I realize the barrel-vault front has no flat vertical face since the elliptical curve is tangentially vertical right at its edge, so the hasp tongue needs to sit against the curved arch surface itself rather than a flat wall—placing it around the point roughly 20° along the arc from the front.

Working out the surface normal at that point so the gold hasp plate can be oriented to lie flush against the curved shell, tilted forward and slightly upward to match the ellipse's tangent direction.

I'll draw the shield outline with its tip pointing toward the lip (+y toward the front lip, which is down when closed), and compute the thickness direction as the cross product of the x and y axes, which gives a vector pointing back/inward symmetrically on both sides.

Actually, I'm reconsidering the hasp placement -- since it's on the lid's outside, it only becomes visible from the back after opening, not from the front. Rather than overcomplicate it, I'll simplify to just a plate with a small gem, then add a gold ornate crest shield with a gem at the lid's back top apex, extruding it along the lid's surface direction so it's visible from behind and above.

Now I'm working out the coin overflow spilling from the chest's front lip, then moving to the crystal clusters -- sweeping hexagonal cross-sections along tilted paths with pointed cone caps at the tips to give them that crystalline look.

I'm using lathe shapes with 6 segments for crisp faceted crystals, varying the tilt angle for each one in a cluster of a tall central crystal surrounded by shorter satellites, keeping the tilted bases just within the dais surface. I'm assigning teal glow colors to the clusters, with some lighter variants mixed in.

For the gold bars, I'm extruding a trapezoid cross-section along the length to get the classic tapered bar shape, then considering adding a stamped label texture on the top face.

Working out the bar positions for the medal stacking pattern...

Now I'm sketching a lathe profile for a bulging sack shape, plotting out the radius points that curve outward then taper at the neck.

Still checking for self-intersections, confirming the mouth opening stays filled solid rather than hollow. I'm adding a crimson rope tie torus around the neck with dangling rope-end rods, plus a decorative patch on the sack front using a coin-and-star glyph in gold on brown, and setting up a mottled burlap texture material.

Now I'm positioning spilled coins poking out of the sack mouth at a tilt, scattering a few extras on the dais near the sack base, and checking the sack's placement against the coin heap and chest to make sure nothing clips — the spacing all works out clear.

I'm verifying the gold bars, crystal clusters, and dais positions all clear each other and the open chest lid with proper margins, and now adding a ring of small gold studs around the dais rim for decorative trim.

Now I'm drafting a goblet-creation function that builds a lathe profile for the cup shape, with parameters for position, color, scale, and optional gem or potion details. Defining the lathe profile points...

Checking that the stem doesn't cross the inner profile confirms things look fine, so I'm moving on to defining the goblet function with parameters for position and fill colors.

Finishing the goblet function: lathing the cup shape, adding a rim torus ring rotated to lie flat, and placing six gems evenly around the cup wall at a fixed radius and angle increment. The torus rotation correctly flips its plane from XY to XZ so the rim sits properly.

For the potion fill, I'm placing a glowing disc slightly inset from the cup's interior wall radius at a given height, nudging the disc radius so it doesn't overlap or leave a visible gap against the lathed inner surface.

I'm also planning small glowing spheres floating above the goblet as magic bubbles, then placing standing goblets at specific positions on the levels and dais, computing their y-heights from the surface height plus offsets.

For each goblet I'm assigning distinct gem and potion colors — magenta potion for the first, cyan for the second, and coins filling the third instead of a potion — then adding small coin shapes clustered inside the cup geometry.

For the fourth goblet I'm checking its placement on the dais, verifying its tilt and position fall within the main heap region using distance and radius calculations so it reads as naturally part of the pile.

Trying to keep the spilled coins from crossing the dais edge as I adjust the goblet's tilt direction, but the math keeps pushing the mouth and spill point too close to the boundary. I'm now considering relocating the tipped goblet to the rear-left instead, though that risks overlapping the coin heap.

Actually, I'll place it on the dais at the right front and bump the dais radius to 1.0 to give more room. Checking the foot position against the L1 and L0 ellipse boundaries confirms it barely clears both.

Let me recompute with a tilted axis direction instead, finding the foot's height on the heap surface and working out where the mouth ends up after the downward tilt—landing around y=0.14.

Checking that the mouth position is clear of the floor with a small margin, so the cup can rest leaning against the coin heap without clipping through it. Now I'm computing spilled coin positions trailing from the cup's mouth down toward the floor, spreading them slightly perpendicular to the flow direction.

Checking the tipped goblet's foot position against L0's falloff, I get a height that puts the mouth slightly above the floor by about 0.05 — it's hovering rather than resting flush, so maybe coins underneath are bridging that gap.

Let me try repositioning the foot further onto the lower heap slope: solving for mouth resting exactly at floor level gives a foot height around 0.243, with a steep ~40° tilt angle from axis to mouth, which seems plausible for something resting against a pile's slope.

Computing the direction vector by solving for the vertical component so the mouth sits at the right height, then splitting the remaining horizontal magnitude between the two axes proportionally, clamping to avoid extreme tilts. For the rim detail I'm orienting a torus along the goblet's axis direction to sit correctly on a tipped goblet.

Now I'm working out the crown geometry: placing its center near the apex of the coin pile, computing the base height so it rests naturally on the slope, checking that the dome's curvature doesn't create gaps at the crown's radius, and setting an exclusion zone so coins don't spawn where the crown sits, leaving room for a ring of coins around its base instead.

Writing lathe profile for crown...

Writing paint logic for engraved chevron pattern...

Now I'm sketching the crown's crest shape with alternating tall and short spikes around the rim, defining their pointed outlines with coordinate arrays.

Still writing spike geometry...

For the gem tips I'm alternating tall spikes between ruby, sapphire, emerald, and amethyst, with shorter spikes getting pearl-white spheres. I'm also adding eight faceted gems around the crown band offset between the spikes, cycling through colors, plus a larger centerpiece ruby with a gold collar at the front.

Now I'm building the crossing arches with gold catmull sweeps rising from the band and meeting at the top, where I'll place a glowing orb to mark the intersection point.

For the orb I'll use a diamond-shaped gem lathe in icy white, topped with a small gold cross made of tiny boxes, and I'm adding a velvet dome inside the crown visible behind the spikes. Finally I'll scatter around 22 gems across the gem heaps and dais with randomized positions, jittered orientations, varying sizes, and mixed colors for a treasure-pile effect.

For the sparkle effect, I'll use double-sided star-shaped cards that face the camera and spin randomly, scattering around 14 of them above the heap in white-gold and cyan tones with varying sizes, floating freely without any connection to the geometry below.

Two star textures in gold and cyan, with cards defaulting to white and needing an explicit root bone passed so they don't snap to the nearest joint like the hinge. I'm positioning the card frame so the star center sits at half the card height, and sketching out the dais studs, rim, and whether a banner or chest label makes sense.

Now I'm adding small embossed details to the chest front—straps with rivets over painted wood—then working out the rivet placement: merging small gold spheres embedded at the strap face positions, spaced across the front, while skipping the central lock area where the straps overlap vertically.

Still placing rivets...

Checking the plate's vertical bounds against the strap positions, I realize the plate tip actually overlaps the lower strap and the strap sits in front of it in z-depth, so I need to shift the plate forward slightly to make sure it reads as being on top.

Now I'm positioning the vertical side straps outside the plate's width and working out the side/back strap box dimensions and depths so they protrude just enough from the outer wall, then sketching a thin gold rim band along the top edge of the body.

Skipping decorative feet for now and focusing instead on front/back loop placement for the straps, confirming coin and detail counts are fine, and sizing the dais rune relative to the dais top radius.

Now I'm generating the SVG for the rune decal, with tick marks around a circle and small glyph chevrons placed radially...

Adding glyph strokes and ring layers...
